modules.title: 01. Go fundamentals
modules.description: Go is used for backends, infrastructure and distributed systems (Docker, Kubernetes and etcd are written in it). Learn its syntax, errors, interfaces and tests.

lessons.title: Go syntax, types, slices, maps, structs and errors
objectives: Install Go, run programs and use `go mod init`, `go run`, `go build`, `go fmt`.
Use variables, functions, slices, maps, structs and methods.
Return and check errors the Go way instead of exceptions.

topics.title: Basics
details: Static types with inference (`x := 5`), functions with multiple return values, `for` as the only loop.
Slices are views over arrays (append may reallocate); maps are hash maps; structs group fields; methods attach to types.

topics.title: Errors
details: Functions return `(value, error)`; check `if err != nil { return ..., fmt.Errorf("loading config: %w", err) }`.
Wrap errors with %w and inspect them with errors.Is / errors.As.

topics.title: Tooling
details: `go fmt` formats everything the same way; `go vet` finds suspicious code; modules pin dependencies in go.mod and go.sum.

reading.locator: A Tour of Go: complete 'Basics' (packages, variables, functions; flow control; more types: structs, slices and maps).

assignment.title: Word frequency CLI in Go
instructions: Create a module `wordfreq` that reads a text file path from the command line and prints the 10 most frequent words.
Return errors for a missing file and an empty file; print them clearly and exit with code 1.
Use a map for counts and sort a slice of structs for the top 10.
deliverables: Go module with README and sample output.
acceptanceCriteria: Missing and empty files produce clear errors and exit code 1.
`go vet` reports nothing.

questions.prompt: How does Go report failures?
questions.answer: By returning an error value that the caller checks.
questions.explanation: There are no exceptions for normal errors.

questions.prompt: What does `append` do when a slice is full?
questions.answer: Allocates a larger array and copies the elements.
questions.explanation: So always use the returned slice.

reviewPrompts: How do you wrap and inspect an error?

lessons.title: Interfaces, packages, testing and goroutines
objectives: Define and satisfy interfaces implicitly.
Write table-driven tests and benchmarks with `go test`.
Run work concurrently with goroutines, channels, sync.WaitGroup and context cancellation.

topics.title: Interfaces
details: A type satisfies an interface by having its methods; no `implements` keyword. Small interfaces (io.Reader) are idiomatic.

topics.title: Testing
details: Files ending in _test.go; table-driven tests loop over cases with t.Run; `go test -race ./...` finds data races.

topics.title: Concurrency
details: `go f()` starts a goroutine; channels pass values safely; `select` waits on several channels.
context.Context carries deadlines and cancellation through calls; every network call should accept one.

reading.locator: A Tour of Go: 'Methods and interfaces' and 'Concurrency' sections, completing every exercise.

assignment.title: Concurrent URL checker
instructions: Write a CLI that checks a list of URLs concurrently with a worker pool of N goroutines and a per-request timeout from context.
Define a `Fetcher` interface so tests use a fake fetcher instead of the network.
Write table-driven tests and run them with -race.
deliverables: Go module, tests and a results table for N = 1, 5, 20.
acceptanceCriteria: Tests pass with -race and use no real network.
Timeouts cancel slow requests.

questions.prompt: How does a Go type implement an interface?
questions.answer: Implicitly, by having all its methods.
questions.explanation: No declaration is needed.

questions.prompt: What does `go test -race` detect?
questions.answer: Data races between goroutines.
questions.explanation: Run it in CI for concurrent code.

reviewPrompts: When would you use a channel versus a mutex?

modules.title: 02. JavaScript and TypeScript fundamentals
modules.description: The language of the web and of Node.js services. Learn modern JavaScript, asynchronous code and TypeScript's type system.

lessons.title: Modern JavaScript: values, functions, objects, modules and async
objectives: Use let/const, arrow functions, destructuring, spread and array methods (map, filter, reduce).
Explain the event loop, promises and async/await.
Organise code with ES modules and run it with Node.js.

topics.title: Language core
details: `const` by default, `let` when reassigning; `===` not `==`; objects and arrays are references.
Array methods replace most loops: `orders.filter(o => o.paid).map(o => o.total)`.

topics.title: Async
details: JavaScript is single-threaded with an event loop; slow work (network, timers) runs asynchronously.
A Promise represents a future value; `await fetch(url)` pauses the function without blocking the program; wrap in try/catch.

topics.title: Modules
details: `export function x` and `import { x } from './x.js'`; npm packages are declared in package.json.

reading.locator: MDN JavaScript Guide: 'Grammar and types', 'Functions', 'Working with objects', 'Using promises' and 'JavaScript modules'.

assignment.title: Async data script
instructions: With Node.js, fetch JSON from two public APIs in parallel with Promise.all and merge the results.
Handle one failing request gracefully with Promise.allSettled.
Split the code into two modules and add a script entry in package.json.
deliverables: Repository with package.json, modules and output.
acceptanceCriteria: Requests run in parallel and a failure does not crash the script.

questions.prompt: What does await do?
questions.answer: Pauses the async function until the promise settles, without blocking the event loop.
questions.explanation: Other work continues meanwhile.

questions.prompt: Difference between == and ===?
questions.answer: === compares without type conversion.
questions.explanation: Use === to avoid surprises.

reviewPrompts: Explain the event loop to a beginner.

lessons.title: TypeScript: types, narrowing, generics and strict mode
objectives: Annotate functions and objects with types, unions and interfaces.
Narrow unions safely with type guards and discriminated unions.
Write generic functions and configure tsconfig with strict mode.

topics.title: Types
details: TypeScript adds compile-time types to JavaScript and is removed at runtime; `tsc --noEmit` checks types.
`type Order = { id: string; total: number; status: 'open' | 'paid' }` documents and checks shapes.

topics.title: Narrowing
details: Use `if (typeof x === 'string')`, `in`, or a `kind` field to narrow a union before using it.
Avoid `any`; use `unknown` for untrusted input and validate it (for example with zod).

topics.title: Generics
details: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` keeps type information through reusable code.

reading.locator: TypeScript Handbook: 'The Basics', 'Everyday Types', 'Narrowing', 'More on Functions' and 'Generics' (under Type Manipulation).

assignment.title: Type a messy JavaScript module
instructions: Convert your async data script to TypeScript with strict mode.
Model API responses as types, validate untrusted JSON at the boundary, and use a discriminated union for success/error results.
Add a generic helper and unit tests (Vitest or Jest).
deliverables: TypeScript project with tsconfig, tests and notes on bugs the compiler found.
acceptanceCriteria: `tsc --noEmit` passes with strict mode and no `any`.
Invalid JSON is rejected with a clear error.

questions.prompt: Do TypeScript types exist at runtime?
questions.answer: No, they are erased when compiled.
questions.explanation: Validate external data at runtime too.

questions.prompt: Why prefer unknown over any?
questions.answer: unknown forces you to check the value before using it.
questions.explanation: any turns off type checking.

reviewPrompts: Write a discriminated union for a payment result.

modules.title: 03. Front-end development with React
modules.description: Build interactive user interfaces with React: components, state, effects, data fetching and front-end testing.

lessons.title: Components, props, state and hooks
objectives: Build a UI from small components that receive props.
Manage state with useState and derive values instead of duplicating state.
Use useEffect correctly and avoid common re-render bugs.

topics.title: Thinking in React
details: Break the UI into components, find the minimal state, decide which component owns it, pass data down and events up.
Rendering must be pure: same props and state produce the same output.

topics.title: Hooks
details: `const [items, setItems] = useState([])`; update immutably (`setItems([...items, x])`).
useEffect synchronises with external systems (subscriptions, timers); include every dependency and clean up.

topics.title: Lists and forms
details: Give list items a stable `key`; controlled inputs keep form values in state.

reading.locator: React Learn: 'Quick Start', 'Thinking in React', 'Describing the UI', 'Adding Interactivity' and 'Managing State'.

assignment.title: Kanban board
instructions: Create a React + TypeScript app (Vite) with columns To do / Doing / Done.
Add, edit, move and delete cards; persist to localStorage with error handling.
Keep state minimal and derive counts per column.
acceptanceCriteria: No duplicated state; counts are derived.
Reloading keeps the cards.

questions.prompt: Why must list items have a key?
questions.answer: So React can match items between renders.
questions.explanation: Use stable IDs, not array indexes, when items move.

questions.prompt: When do you need useEffect?
questions.answer: To synchronise with something outside React, such as a subscription or timer.
questions.explanation: Not for deriving values from state.

lessons.title: Data fetching, routing and front-end testing
objectives: Fetch from an API with loading and error states.
Add client-side routing and forms with validation.
Test components with Testing Library and user flows with Playwright.

topics.title: Data
details: Every request has three UI states: loading, error, success. Cancel or ignore stale responses when inputs change.
Libraries like TanStack Query add caching and retries; learn the manual way first.

topics.title: Routing and forms
details: React Router maps URLs to pages; validate forms on the client and again on the server.

topics.title: Testing
details: Component tests render and click like a user (`getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })`).
End-to-end tests with Playwright run the real app in a browser; keep a few critical flows.

reading.locator: Full Stack Open part 2 'Communicating with server' and part 5 'Testing React apps' (including end-to-end testing).

assignment.title: Movie search app
instructions: Build a search page that calls a public movie or books API with debounced input, loading and error states.
Add a details route and a favourites list.
Write three component tests and one Playwright test for search -> details -> favourite.
deliverables: Repository with tests running in CI.
acceptanceCriteria: Tests pass in CI.
Slow or failed requests show proper UI states.

questions.prompt: What three states does every data fetch need in the UI?
questions.answer: Loading, error and success.
questions.explanation: Users must see what is happening.

questions.prompt: Should you trust client-side validation alone?
questions.answer: No, always validate on the server too.
questions.explanation: Clients can be bypassed.

reviewPrompts: How do you avoid showing a stale response?

modules.title: 04. Node.js services and real-time communication
modules.description: Build HTTP and WebSocket servers in Node.js, broadcast updates between server instances, and handle connection failures.

lessons.title: HTTP servers, middleware and persistence in Node.js
objectives: Build a REST API with Express or Fastify, including validation and error handling.
Connect to PostgreSQL with a pool and parameterised queries.
Structure a service into routes, services and data access layers with tests.

topics.title: Server basics
details: A route handler receives a request and returns a response; middleware runs in between (logging, auth, JSON parsing).
Validate request bodies (zod) and return consistent error JSON with correct status codes.

topics.title: Data
details: Use a connection pool (pg) and parameterised queries; never build SQL strings from input.

topics.title: Structure and tests
details: Keep handlers thin; put business rules in services that can be tested without HTTP.
Supertest calls your app in-process for API tests.

reading.locator: Full Stack Open part 3 'Programming a server with NodeJS and Express' and part 4 'Testing Express servers, user administration'.

assignment.title: Notes API
instructions: Build a TypeScript notes API with CRUD, validation, pagination and PostgreSQL via Docker Compose.
Write service unit tests and API tests with Supertest against a test database.
deliverables: Repository with compose file, tests and OpenAPI description.
acceptanceCriteria: Invalid input returns 400 with a clear error.
Tests run against a fresh database in CI.

questions.prompt: What is middleware?
questions.answer: Code that runs between receiving a request and the route handler.
questions.explanation: Used for logging, auth, parsing.

questions.prompt: Why keep business logic out of route handlers?
questions.answer: So it can be tested without HTTP and reused.
questions.explanation: Handlers just translate HTTP to service calls.

reviewPrompts: How do you test against a real database in CI?

lessons.title: WebSockets, pub/sub and scaling real-time servers
objectives: Explain WebSockets versus HTTP polling and server-sent events.
Build a WebSocket server with rooms, heartbeats and reconnection.
Fan out messages across several server instances with Redis pub/sub.

topics.title: Protocol
details: A WebSocket upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent two-way channel; ideal for chat, collaboration and live dashboards.

topics.title: Reliability
details: Connections drop; send heartbeats (ping/pong), reconnect with backoff, and resend missed messages using sequence numbers.

topics.title: Scaling
details: Clients connected to different servers need a shared channel: publish to Redis, every server subscribes and forwards to its clients.
Load balancers must support long-lived connections (sticky sessions or connection-aware routing).

reading.locator: RFC 6455 sections 1.1-1.3 (overview and opening handshake) and section 5.5.2-5.5.3 (ping and pong).

assignment.title: Multi-server chat
instructions: Build a WebSocket chat with rooms using the ws library.
Run two server instances behind different ports and connect them with Redis pub/sub.
Add heartbeats and client reconnection that fetches missed messages by sequence number.
Measure message latency with 50 scripted clients.
deliverables: Repository, load script and latency results.
acceptanceCriteria: Clients on different servers see each other's messages.
A reconnecting client receives missed messages.

questions.prompt: Why do multiple WebSocket servers need pub/sub?
questions.answer: Clients on different servers must receive the same messages.
questions.explanation: Redis pub/sub broadcasts between servers.

questions.prompt: How do you detect a dead WebSocket connection?
questions.answer: Heartbeat ping/pong with a timeout.
questions.explanation: TCP alone may not notice quickly.

reviewPrompts: How would you avoid losing messages on reconnect?

modules.title: 05. API design: REST, OpenAPI and gRPC
modules.description: Design APIs that are easy to use and safe to evolve: resource modelling, errors, pagination, versioning, OpenAPI contracts and gRPC services.

lessons.title: Designing REST APIs with OpenAPI
objectives: Model resources, URLs, methods and status codes consistently.
Design pagination, filtering, error format and idempotent retries.
Write an OpenAPI specification and generate documentation from it.

topics.title: Design rules
details: Nouns in URLs, plural collections (`/orders`), nested only one level (`/orders/{id}/items`).
Cursor pagination (`?cursor=...&limit=50`) is stable when data changes; offset pagination is simpler but can skip rows.

topics.title: Errors and safety
details: One error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "insufficient_funds", "message": "..." } }`.
Accept an `Idempotency-Key` header on POST so clients can retry safely.

topics.title: Evolution
details: Add optional fields freely; never rename or remove fields without a new version; deprecate with dates.
OpenAPI documents the contract so clients, tests and docs come from one source.

reading.locator: Swagger docs: 'What Is OpenAPI?', 'Basic Structure', 'Paths and Operations', 'Describing Parameters' and 'Describing Responses'.

assignment.title: Design an orders API
instructions: Write an OpenAPI 3 spec for an orders service: create, get, list with cursor pagination, cancel.
Define the error format and idempotency behaviour.
Render docs with Swagger UI or Redoc and review your design against the rules in this lesson.
deliverables: openapi.yaml and a one-page design rationale.
acceptanceCriteria: The spec validates with an OpenAPI linter.
Pagination and idempotency are specified exactly.

questions.prompt: Why prefer cursor pagination for changing data?
questions.answer: It does not skip or repeat rows when items are inserted.
questions.explanation: Offsets shift when data changes.

questions.prompt: Is removing a response field a breaking change?
questions.answer: Yes.
questions.explanation: Clients may depend on it; version or deprecate first.

reviewPrompts: Design URLs for users, orders and items.

lessons.title: gRPC and Protocol Buffers
objectives: Define services and messages in proto3 and generate Go code.
Implement unary and server-streaming RPCs with deadlines.
Evolve messages without breaking clients.

topics.title: Why gRPC
details: Binary protobuf messages over HTTP/2: smaller and faster than JSON, with generated typed clients; common between internal services.

topics.title: Defining services
details: `service KV { rpc Get(GetRequest) returns (GetReply); }`; field numbers identify fields on the wire and must never be reused.

topics.title: Robust calls
details: Always set deadlines; map errors to gRPC status codes (NOT_FOUND, UNAVAILABLE); retry only idempotent calls.

reading.locator: gRPC docs: 'Introduction to gRPC', 'Core concepts' and the Go 'Quick start' and 'Basics tutorial'.

assignment.title: Key-value service over gRPC
instructions: Define a KV service (Get, Put, Delete, Watch as server streaming) in proto3.
Implement it in Go with an in-memory map and a mutex; write a client CLI.
Add deadlines and test that a slow server returns DEADLINE_EXCEEDED.
Add a new optional field and prove an old client still works.
deliverables: Repository with proto, server, client and tests.
acceptanceCriteria: Deadline test passes.
Old client compatibility is demonstrated.

questions.prompt: Why must protobuf field numbers never be reused?
questions.answer: They identify fields on the wire; reuse corrupts data for old clients.
questions.explanation: Reserve removed numbers.

questions.prompt: Why set a deadline on every RPC?
questions.answer: So callers do not wait forever and resources are freed.
questions.explanation: Deadlines propagate across services.

reviewPrompts: REST or gRPC for a public API? For internal services?

modules.title: 06. Distributed systems fundamentals
modules.description: What changes when a program runs on many machines: replication, consistency models, consensus with Raft, time and failure handling.

lessons.title: Replication, consistency models and linearizability
objectives: Explain synchronous and asynchronous replication and their failure trade-offs.
Distinguish linearizable, sequential, causal and eventual consistency.
Check a history of operations for linearizability with a tool.

topics.title: Replication
details: Copies of data on several machines give fault tolerance and read scaling; the hard part is keeping them in agreement.
Async replication is fast but can lose acknowledged writes on failover; sync is safer but slower.

topics.title: Consistency models
details: Linearizable: the system behaves like one copy and every read sees the latest completed write. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop.
Stronger models are easier to program against and cost more latency and availability.

topics.title: Testing
details: Record each client operation's start, end and result; a checker (Porcupine, Knossos) searches for a valid single-copy order.

reading.locator: Jepsen 'Consistency Models': read the overview and the pages for linearizable, sequential and eventual consistency.

assignment.title: Break a naive replicated store
instructions: Build a Go key-value store with one primary and two async replicas using HTTP or gRPC.
Write a test harness that partitions the primary and promotes a replica; record client histories.
Show a lost acknowledged write and explain which consistency guarantee was violated.
acceptanceCriteria: The violation is reproduced from a fixed seed.

questions.prompt: What does linearizability guarantee?
questions.answer: Operations appear to happen instantly in an order consistent with real time, as if on one copy.
questions.explanation: Every read sees the latest completed write.

questions.prompt: Risk of asynchronous replication?
questions.answer: Acknowledged writes can be lost on failover.
questions.explanation: The replica may not have received them yet.

reviewPrompts: Compare linearizable and eventual consistency with an example.

lessons.title: Consensus with Raft
objectives: Explain leader election, log replication and the commit rule in Raft.
Explain why a majority quorum prevents split-brain.
Implement leader election in Go with a simulated network.

topics.title: Roles and terms
details: Each node is a follower, candidate or leader; terms are logical clocks. A candidate wins with votes from a majority.
Randomised election timeouts make split votes unlikely.

topics.title: Log replication
details: The leader appends entries and sends AppendEntries; an entry is committed once stored on a majority, then applied to the state machine.
The log-matching check makes followers' logs identical to the leader's.

topics.title: Safety
details: Any two majorities overlap, so a new leader always has every committed entry (election restriction).
Persist currentTerm, votedFor and the log before replying to RPCs.

reading.locator: Raft paper (extended version): sections 5.1 'Raft basics', 5.2 'Leader election', 5.3 'Log replication', 5.4 'Safety' and Figure 2 (keep it next to your code).

assignment.title: Raft leader election
instructions: Implement Raft leader election and heartbeats in Go over a simulated network you control.
Test: one leader is elected; killing the leader elects a new one; a node in a minority partition cannot become leader.
Use the raft.github.io visualisation to check your understanding of each scenario.
deliverables: Code and passing tests (run 500 times with random seeds).
acceptanceCriteria: No test run ever shows two leaders in the same term.

questions.prompt: When is a Raft log entry committed?
questions.answer: When the leader has stored it on a majority of servers (in its current term).
questions.explanation: Then it can be applied.

questions.prompt: Why randomise election timeouts?
questions.answer: To avoid repeated split votes.
questions.explanation: One node usually times out first and wins.

reviewPrompts: Draw a 5-node cluster during a partition.
What must be persisted before replying?

lessons.title: Time, failure and idempotency in distributed systems
objectives: Explain why clocks disagree and use logical clocks for ordering.
Handle timeouts, retries and duplicates with idempotent operations.
Apply fault-injection testing to find bugs before users do.

topics.title: Time
details: Physical clocks drift and jump; do not order events across machines by wall-clock timestamps alone.
Lamport clocks and version vectors capture happened-before; Raft terms are a logical clock too.

topics.title: Failures
details: A timeout means 'unknown', not 'failed': the request may have succeeded. Retrying can duplicate work unless operations are idempotent.
Use request IDs so servers apply each request once.

topics.title: Testing
details: Inject delays, drops, duplicates and crashes in tests; run with many seeds; keep the failing seed as a regression test.

reading.locator: raft.github.io: run the interactive visualisation with message drops and node crashes, then read the 'Client interaction' section (section 8) of the Raft paper.

assignment.title: Exactly-once effect with retries
instructions: Add client request IDs to your KV store so retried Put requests are applied once.
Inject random message duplication and loss; prove the final state is correct across 1,000 seeded runs.
acceptanceCriteria: No duplicated effects across all runs.

questions.prompt: What does a timeout tell the client?
questions.answer: Nothing certain: the request may or may not have been applied.
questions.explanation: So retries must be safe.

questions.prompt: How do you make retries safe?
questions.answer: Make operations idempotent, for example with request IDs.
questions.explanation: The server ignores duplicates.

reviewPrompts: Why not order events by wall clock?
Explain request IDs for exactly-once effects.

modules.title: 07. Storage engines: B-trees and LSM-trees
modules.description: How databases store data on disk, and why write-heavy systems use log-structured merge trees.

lessons.title: Write-ahead logs, B-trees, LSM-trees and Bloom filters
objectives: Explain the write-ahead log and crash recovery.
Compare B-trees and LSM-trees for reads, writes and space.
Implement a small LSM store with memtable, SSTables, compaction and Bloom filters.

topics.title: Durability
details: Write the change to an append-only log and fsync before acknowledging; after a crash, replay the log.

topics.title: B-trees vs LSM
details: B-trees update pages in place: fast reads, random writes. LSM-trees buffer writes in memory (memtable), flush sorted files (SSTables) and merge them later (compaction): fast writes, more read work.
Write amplification, read amplification and space amplification are the trade-off triangle.

topics.title: Bloom filters
details: A Bloom filter says 'definitely not here' or 'maybe here', letting reads skip SSTables; false positives possible, false negatives impossible.

reading.locator: RocksDB Overview wiki page: sections on the high-level architecture, MemTable, Write-Ahead Log, SST files, compaction and Bloom filters.

assignment.title: Mini LSM store
instructions: Implement in Go: WAL append and replay, memtable (sorted map), flush to immutable SSTable files, read path newest-first, tombstones for deletes.
Add size-tiered compaction and a Bloom filter per SSTable.
Crash-test: kill the process at random points and verify no acknowledged write is lost.
deliverables: Code, tests and a short design note.
acceptanceCriteria: Deleted keys stay deleted after compaction.
Bloom filters never give false negatives in tests.

questions.prompt: Why do LSM-trees write fast?
questions.answer: Writes are buffered in memory and flushed sequentially.
questions.explanation: Sequential I/O is much faster than random updates.

questions.prompt: Can a Bloom filter return a false negative?
questions.answer: No.
questions.explanation: It can only return false positives.

modules.title: 08. Collaborative editing and CRDTs
modules.description: How apps like Google Docs and Figma let many people edit at once and merge changes without conflicts.

lessons.title: CRDTs and operational transformation
objectives: Explain why naive last-writer-wins loses edits in collaborative text.
Explain how sequence CRDTs (RGA/YATA) give each character a unique ID and merge concurrently.
Implement a simple text CRDT and prove convergence with property tests.

topics.title: The problem
details: Two users type at the same position while offline; when they reconnect, both edits must survive and every replica must end with identical text.

topics.title: Approaches
details: Operational transformation (OT) transforms operations against each other on a central server.
CRDTs give each element a unique, ordered ID so merges are commutative and need no central server.

topics.title: Practical concerns
details: Tombstones keep deleted characters' IDs; periodic snapshots and garbage collection keep memory bounded.
Presence (cursors) is ephemeral and sent separately from document state.

reading.locator: crdt.tech: read the 'Introduction' resources and the paper 'A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types' (sections on registers, counters and sequences).

assignment.title: Text CRDT with property tests
instructions: Implement an RGA-style text CRDT in TypeScript (insert, delete, merge, encode).
Write fast-check property tests: random concurrent operations delivered in random orders always converge.
Connect it to your WebSocket server so two browser tabs edit together, including offline edits.
deliverables: Library, tests and a demo GIF.
acceptanceCriteria: Thousands of random histories converge.
Offline edits merge without loss.

questions.prompt: Why does last-writer-wins fail for text editing?
questions.answer: It discards one user's concurrent edits.
questions.explanation: Collaborative editing must keep both.

questions.prompt: What makes CRDT merges conflict-free?
questions.answer: Operations commute because every element has a unique ordered ID.
questions.explanation: Order of delivery does not change the result.

modules.title: 09. System design interviews
modules.description: Prepare for SDE system design rounds: a repeatable framework, capacity estimation and classic designs explained with trade-offs.

lessons.title: A repeatable system design interview framework
objectives: Run a 45-minute design interview: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high level, deep dive, wrap-up.
Estimate QPS, storage and bandwidth quickly.
Communicate trade-offs and respond to interviewer hints.

topics.title: Framework
details: 5 min requirements (functional, non-functional, scale), 5 min estimates, 5 min API and data model, 15 min high-level design, 10 min deep dive, 5 min bottlenecks and failures.

topics.title: Estimation
details: Daily active users x actions per user / 86,400 = average QPS; multiply by 2-10 for peak. Storage = items per day x size x retention.

topics.title: Communication
details: Think aloud, state assumptions, offer options and choose one with a reason; ask what the interviewer wants to go deeper on.

reading.locator: System Design Primer: 'System design interview questions with solutions' (Pastebin and Twitter timeline walkthroughs) and 'Appendix: Powers of two table' and 'Latency numbers every programmer should know'.

assignment.title: Two timed designs
instructions: Do two 45-minute timed designs (a chat app and a news feed) on paper or a whiteboard tool.
Write each up afterwards with estimates and trade-offs; compare with the primer's solutions and note gaps.
deliverables: Two design write-ups with diagrams and self-review.
acceptanceCriteria: Each has numeric estimates and at least three justified trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What comes first in a design interview?
questions.answer: Clarifying requirements and scale.
questions.explanation: Designing without them solves the wrong problem.

questions.prompt: Average QPS for 10M daily users doing 20 actions each?
questions.answer: About 2,300 per second.

reviewPrompts: What deep dives could follow a news feed design?

lessons.title: Classic designs: rate limiter, chat, news feed, URL shortener and key-value store
objectives: Explain the key components and trade-offs of five frequently asked designs.
Choose storage, caching and messaging for each with reasons.
Identify the main failure modes and mitigations for each.

topics.title: Rate limiter
details: Token bucket in Redis with atomic Lua; per-user and per-IP keys; return 429 with Retry-After.

topics.title: Chat and feed
details: Chat: WebSockets, per-conversation ordered storage, delivery receipts, fan-out via pub/sub.
Feed: fan-out on write for normal users, fan-out on read for celebrities, cached timelines.

topics.title: Key-value store
details: Consistent hashing for partitioning, replication with quorums (R + W > N), hinted handoff and anti-entropy.

reading.locator: System Design 101: sections on rate limiting, caching, message queues, consistent hashing and the case studies.

assignment.title: Design flashcards and a mock
instructions: Make a one-page summary per design: requirements, diagram, data model, scaling, failure modes.
Do one mock interview with a friend or record yourself, using a design you have not prepared.
deliverables: Five summaries and the mock self-review.
acceptanceCriteria: Each summary names at least two failure modes with mitigations.

questions.prompt: What does R + W > N guarantee in quorum systems?
questions.answer: Every read quorum overlaps the latest write quorum.
questions.explanation: So reads can see the latest write.

questions.prompt: Fan-out on write or read for celebrities?
questions.answer: Fan-out on read.
questions.explanation: Writing to millions of followers' timelines is too expensive.

reviewPrompts: How does consistent hashing reduce data movement?

modules.title: 10. Developer tools with LLM APIs
modules.description: Build software that uses language models responsibly: API calls, structured output, webhooks and GitHub Apps.

lessons.title: Calling LLM APIs, structured output and building a GitHub App
objectives: Call an LLM API with system prompts, structured JSON output and token limits.
Build a GitHub App that receives verified webhooks and comments on pull requests.
Control cost and failure with caching, timeouts and schema validation.

topics.title: LLM API basics
details: Send messages with a system prompt; ask for JSON matching a schema and validate it before use.
Tokens cost money: cache by input hash, limit context, set max tokens and timeouts.

topics.title: GitHub Apps
details: An App has a private key and fine-grained permissions; it receives webhooks (verify the signature) and acts with short-lived installation tokens.
Process webhooks asynchronously and idempotently by delivery ID.

topics.title: Responsibility
details: Never send code you do not own to an external API; keep keys in secrets; show model output as suggestions, not facts.

reading.locator: GitHub Docs: 'About creating GitHub Apps', then 'Building a GitHub App that responds to webhook events' and 'Validating webhook deliveries'.

assignment.title: Review-comment prototype
instructions: Create a private GitHub App on a test repository with pull_request events.
On each PR, send the diff to an LLM asking for JSON comments (file, line, message); validate and post them.
Cache by diff hash, handle invalid JSON and timeouts, and log token usage.
deliverables: Repository, setup README and screenshots of comments.
acceptanceCriteria: Invalid model output never reaches GitHub.
Re-delivered webhooks do not duplicate comments.

questions.prompt: Why validate LLM JSON output?
questions.answer: Models can return malformed or wrong-shaped data.
questions.explanation: Treat it as untrusted input.

questions.prompt: How does a GitHub App prove a webhook is genuine?
questions.answer: By verifying the HMAC signature header with the webhook secret.
questions.explanation: Reject unsigned requests.

reviewPrompts: List three ways to reduce LLM cost.

modules.title: 11. Working like a senior engineer
modules.description: The habits that get engineers promoted: effective code review, testing strategy, design reviews, on-call and ownership.

lessons.title: Code review, testing strategy, on-call and ownership
objectives: Give and receive code review that improves design, not just style.
Choose a test mix (unit, integration, end-to-end) for a service.
Prepare for on-call: alerts, runbooks, incident roles and blameless postmortems.

topics.title: Code review
details: Look at design, correctness, tests, readability, then style. Be specific and kind; explain why.
Authors: small PRs, clear descriptions, respond to every comment.

topics.title: Testing strategy
details: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against real dependencies, a handful of end-to-end tests for critical journeys.

topics.title: Operations
details: Alert on user-visible symptoms; every alert links a runbook. After incidents, write blameless postmortems with action items.

reading.locator: Google Engineering Practices: 'The Standard of Code Review', 'What to look for in a code review' and 'The CL author's guide'.

assignment.title: Review and runbook
instructions: Review two open-source pull requests (read-only) and write the comments you would leave, ordered by importance.
Write a test strategy and an on-call runbook for one of your projects.
deliverables: Review notes, test strategy and runbook.
acceptanceCriteria: Review comments focus on design and correctness before style.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer check first?
questions.answer: Design and correctness.
questions.explanation: Style is the least important and best automated.

questions.prompt: What is a blameless postmortem?
questions.answer: An incident review that focuses on systems and fixes, not on blaming people.
questions.explanation: It encourages honest reporting.

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Write small, tested programs in Go and TypeScript.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Repositories with passing tests and a README for each exercise.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Build a React front end and a Node.js or Go service that talk over well-designed REST, gRPC or WebSocket APIs.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A working full-stack app with automated unit and end-to-end tests.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Explain and implement replication, consensus, storage engines and conflict-free merging.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Your own Raft and LSM implementations passing failure tests, plus a CRDT with convergence tests.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Design systems in interviews, build developer tools with LLM APIs and work like a senior engineer.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Mock system-design write-ups, a working GitHub App and reviewed pull requests.
